newsitem.title: USA: Texas losses pose warning signs for Republicans.
newsitem.headline: Texas losses pose warning signs for Republicans.

text.p: Republican losses in two House elections in Texas Tuesday illustrate the danger to the party of a growing ideological rift between ultra-conservative activists and more moderate members.

In runoff elections, Democratic challenger Nick Lampson defeated freshman Republican Representative Steve Stockman in the 9th Congressional District. Stockman, one of the most right-wing members of Congress, had been criticised for close ties to right-wing militia groups after the Oklahoma City bombing.

In the 25th Congressional District, Democratic incumbent Ken Bentsen won re-election after conservative Christians refused to rally behind Republican candidate Dolly Madison McKenna, who strongly backs abortion rights.
Christian leaders had advised supporters either to cast blank ballots or stay home. Many appear to have done so since turnout was extremely light.

"The people of Texas have sent a message to Washington that they do not want the extremist Republican agenda of the last two years to surface again," said a happy Dick Gephardt, the Democratic House minority leader.

Although the elections did not change the fact that Republicans will retain a 20-seat majority in the House, they should provide a wake-up call, said University of Texas political scientist Bruce Buchanan.
"The Republicans shot themselves in the foot. The Bentsen seat was theirs for the taking if they had only united behind their candidate," he said.

It would be a mistake to overestimate Republican problems. The nation still appears to be on a conservative trend and the party has bright prospects of adding to its congressional majorities in the 1998 elections.

However, something of a vacuum is appearing in the political centre, which Democrats led by President Clinton are seeking to fill. The more the Republicans move to the right, the more they risk ceding that vital political territory.
In recent years, Texas has become one of the most Republican states in the nation and in another election held Tuesday the party took control of the state Senate for the first time in 24 years.
But Democrats retained a slim majority in the state's congressional delegation, when logic would suggest that Republicans ought to hold a 55-60 percent edge.

"The Republican Party has a key segment, in the shape of Christian conservatives, who refuse to accept that their party is a big tent and that's going to hold them back with moderate voters," Buchanan said.
As long as strong anti-abortion activists insist on ideological purity and nominate ultra-conservative candidates for national office, Republicans may lose other winnable seats in future elections.
In last month's congressional elections, right-wing Republicans lost several races across the nation that more moderate candidates might have won.
For example, in the conservative state of North Carolina, where the Christian Coalition controls the Republican Party, the party actually lost some ground.

"They put forward a much more morally conservative ticket than anybody had ever seen before here and were defeated up and down the state," said Michael Lienesch, an expert on the Christian Coalition at the University of North Carolina.

On election night, Christian activists and Republican moderates engaged in a fist fight at a celebration for North Carolina's Republican candidate for governor, Robin Hayes, with each side blaming the other for his defeat.

"Republicans here are badly divided and unsure where to go next. Even the Christian Coalition is becoming divided between those who are adamant about opposition to abortion and those who want to downplay the issue," Lienesch said.
